steps.name: prompt
steps.text: Write the introduction for our DePT (Decoupled Prompt Tuning) paper. Cover vision-language models and prompt tuning, the base-new tradeoff problem, our channel-bias analysis and the DePT framework, its flexibility and results across baselines, and a contributions list.

steps.name: skeleton_outline
steps.text:
- Vision-language pre-trained models and their limits
- Prompt tuning and the Base-New Tradeoff (BNT)
- DePT: channel bias analysis and decoupling
- Flexibility and effectiveness
- Contributions

steps.name: detailed_outline
steps.text:
- VLPMs and their limits
  - remarkable progress in large VLPMs recently
  - CLIP: contrastive loss aligns images and textual descriptions in common feature space
  - captures open-set visual concepts, but zero-shot generalization greatly reduced under severe category / distribution / domain shift between upstream data and downstream tasks
- Prompt tuning and BNT
  - inspired by prompt engineering in NLP; Prompt Tuning (Context Optimization)
  - parameter-efficient; optimize task-specific prompt (trainable vectors) with handful of base (target) task data; VLPM weights frozen
  - BNT dilemma: better on base task -> worse on new tasks (unseen classes), and vice versa
  - numerous efforts: anti-overfitting strategies during prompt tuning
  - BNT far from resolved; mechanisms poorly understood
- DePT
  - Decoupled Prompt Tuning: first framework for BNT from feature decoupling perspective
  - analysis of feature channels of base/new tasks from standard Image Text Matching (ITM) head
  - BNT stems from channel bias: most channels occupied by base-specific knowledge -> collapse of task-shared knowledge important to new tasks (Section 2.2)
  - strategy: decouple base-specific and task-shared knowledge in feature channels during prompt tuning
  - Channel Adjusted Transfer (CAT) head: mine base-specific knowledge in isolated feature space; preserve task-shared knowledge in original space; better zero-shot generalization on new tasks (Section 2.3)
  - fuse both at inference -> remarkable boost on base task (Section 3.2)
- Flexibility and effectiveness
  - orthogonal to existing prompt tuning methods
  - baselines: visual VPT; textual CoOp, CoCoOp, KgCoOp; multi-model MaPLe, PromptSRC
  - 11 diverse datasets; consistent improvement regardless of category / distribution / domain shift (Section 3.3)
  - six baselines improved without tradeoffs; absolute gains 1.31 % \thicksim 3.17 % base, 0.71 % \thicksim 2.23 % new, averaged on 11 datasets (Figure 1)
- Contributions
  - 1) analysis of BNT: first to show it stems from channel bias
  - 2) DePT framework, feature decoupling, orthogonal to existing methods
  - 3) experiments on 11 datasets, consistent gains over broad spectrum of baselines

steps.name: partial_draft
steps.text:
In recent years there has been remarkable progress in large vision-language pre-trained models (VLPMs). One big success is the contrastive language-image pretraining (CLIP) model, which uses a contrastive loss as learning objective so that images and their textual descriptions are aligned in a common feature space. VLPMs can capture open-set visual concepts, but their zero-shot generalization performance goes down a lot when there is a severe category shift, distribution shift or domain shift between the upstream training data and the downstream tasks.

Prompt Tuning (also called Context Optimization) was inspired by the success of prompt engineering in NLP and has become a parameter-efficient learning paradigm to adapt powerful VLPMs to downstream tasks. It optimizes a task-specific prompt (i.e., a set of trainable vectors) with a handful of training data from the base (target) task, and the weights of the VLPMs are kept frozen. The advantages are remarkable, but existing prompt tuning methods usually can not escape the Base-New Tradeoff (BNT) dilemma, i.e., the better the tuned/adapted model generalizes to the base task, the worse it generalizes to new tasks (with unseen classes), and the other way around. In recent years there were numerous efforts to reduce the performance degradation of tuned models on new tasks by developing anti-overfitting strategies during prompt tuning. But the BNT problem is still far from solved and its underlying mechanisms are poorly understood.

- DePT
  - Decoupled Prompt Tuning: first framework for BNT from feature decoupling perspective
  - analysis of feature channels from standard Image Text Matching (ITM) head -> channel bias: most channels occupied by base-specific knowledge, task-shared knowledge collapses (Section 2.2)
  - decouple base-specific and task-shared knowledge during prompt tuning
  - Channel Adjusted Transfer (CAT) head: isolated feature space for base-specific knowledge; preserve task-shared knowledge; better zero-shot on new tasks (Section 2.3)
  - fuse at inference -> base task boost (Section 3.2)
- Flexibility and effectiveness
  - orthogonal to existing methods; baselines VPT, CoOp, CoCoOp, KgCoOp, MaPLe, PromptSRC
  - 11 diverse datasets; consistent gains under category / distribution / domain shift (Section 3.3)
  - no tradeoffs: 1.31 % \thicksim 3.17 % base, 0.71 % \thicksim 2.23 % new, averaged on 11 datasets (Figure 1)
- Contributions
  - 1) BNT stems from channel bias (first to show); 2) DePT, orthogonal; 3) experiments on 11 datasets

steps.name: rough_draft
steps.text:
In recent years there has been remarkable progress in large vision-language pre-trained models (VLPMs). One big success is the contrastive language-image pretraining (CLIP) model, which uses a contrastive loss as learning objective so that images and their textual descriptions are aligned in a common feature space. VLPMs can capture open-set visual concepts, but their zero-shot generalization performance goes down a lot when there is a severe category shift, distribution shift or domain shift between the upstream training data and the downstream tasks.

Prompt Tuning (also called Context Optimization) was inspired by the success of prompt engineering in NLP and has become a parameter-efficient learning paradigm to adapt powerful VLPMs to downstream tasks. It optimizes a task-specific prompt (i.e., a set of trainable vectors) with a handful of training data from the base (target) task, and the weights of the VLPMs are kept frozen. The advantages are remarkable, but existing prompt tuning methods usually can not escape the Base-New Tradeoff (BNT) dilemma, i.e., the better the tuned/adapted model generalizes to the base task, the worse it generalizes to new tasks (with unseen classes), and the other way around. In recent years there were numerous efforts to reduce the performance degradation of tuned models on new tasks by developing anti-overfitting strategies during prompt tuning. But the BNT problem is still far from solved and its underlying mechanisms are poorly understood.

In this work we bridge this gap and propose Decoupled Prompt Tuning (DePT), which is a first framework that tackles the BNT problem in prompt tuning from a feature decoupling perspective. We do an in-depth analysis of the feature channels of base and new tasks that are learned by the standard Image Text Matching (ITM) head, and we find that the BNT comes from a channel bias issue: the vast majority of feature channels are occupied by base-specific knowledge (i.e., task-specific knowledge of the base task), and this leads to the collapse of task-shared knowledge that is important for new tasks (Section 2.2). Because of this, the direct strategy to tackle the BNT problem is to decouple base-specific knowledge and task-shared knowledge in feature channels during prompt tuning. To do this, we introduce a Channel Adjusted Transfer (CAT) head that encourages mining base-specific knowledge from feature channels in an isolated feature space, so that task-shared knowledge is preserved in the original feature space and zero-shot generalization performance on new tasks is improved (Section 2.3). Also, by simply fusing base-specific knowledge and task-shared knowledge in the two feature spaces at inference, we boost the performance on the base task remarkably (Section 3.2).

Flexibility and Effectiveness. Our DePT framework is orthogonal to existing prompt tuning methods, so it can be used flexibly to overcome the BNT problem for them. We evaluate DePT with a broad spectrum of baseline methods: the visual prompt tuning method VPT, the textual prompt tuning methods CoOp, CoCoOp and KgCoOp, and the multi-model prompt tuning methods MaPLe and PromptSRC. The experimental results on 11 diverse datasets show that DePT consistently improves the performance of those methods, no matter if there is a category shift, distribution shift or domain shift between base and new tasks, and this shows the strong flexibility and effectiveness of DePT (Section 3.3). DePT enhances the six baselines without performance tradeoffs on base and new tasks – it achieves absolute gains of 1.31 % \thicksim 3.17 % on base tasks and 0.71 % \thicksim 2.23 % on new tasks, averaged on the 11 datasets (Figure 1).

Contributions. We have three main contributions. 1) We give an analysis of the BNT problem in prompt tuning and show for the first time that the BNT comes from the channel bias issue. 2) We propose the DePT framework to tackle the BNT problem from a feature decoupling perspective, and DePT is orthogonal to existing prompt tuning methods. 3) We do experiments on 11 diverse datasets and show that DePT consistently improves the performance of a broad spectrum of baseline methods.

steps.name: revised_draft
steps.text:
Recent years have witnessed remarkable progress in large vision-language pre-trained models (VLPMs). One of the most striking successes is the contrastive language-image pretraining (CLIP) [1] model, which formulates the learning objective as a contrastive loss to align images and their textual descriptions in a common feature space. Despite their ability to capture open-set visual concepts, the zero-shot generalization performance of VLPMs is greatly reduced when there is a severe category shift, distribution shift, or domain shift between upstream training data and downstream tasks.

Inspired by the success of prompt engineering in NLP, Prompt Tuning (or, Context Optimization [2]) has emerged as a parameter-efficient learning paradigm to adapt powerful VLPMs to downstream tasks, by optimizing a task-specific prompt (i.e., a set of trainable vectors) with a handful of training data from the base (target) task while keeping the weights of VLPMs frozen. Despite remarkable advantages, existing prompt tuning methods usually fail to escape the Base-New Tradeoff (BNT) dilemma, i.e., the better the tuned/adapted model generalizes to the base task, the worse it generalizes to new tasks (with unseen classes), and vice versa. Numerous efforts [3,4,5] in recent years have tried to alleviate the performance degradation of tuned models on new tasks by developing anti-overfitting strategies during prompt tuning. Nevertheless, the BNT problem is still far from resolved and its underlying mechanisms remain poorly understood.

In this work, we bridge the gap by proposing Decoupled Prompt Tuning (DePT), a first framework that tackles the BNT problem in prompt tuning from a feature decoupling perspective. Specifically, through an in-depth analysis of the feature channels of base and new tasks learned by the standard Image Text Matching (ITM) head, we find that the BNT stems from a channel bias issue: the vast majority of feature channels are occupied by base-specific knowledge (i.e., task-specific knowledge of the base task), resulting in the collapse of task-shared knowledge important to new tasks (Section 2.2). Inspired by this, a direct strategy to tackle the BNT problem is to decouple base-specific knowledge and task-shared knowledge in feature channels during prompt tuning. To this end, we introduce a Channel Adjusted Transfer (CAT) head that encourages mining base-specific knowledge from feature channels in an isolated feature space, thereby facilitating the preservation of task-shared knowledge in the original feature space and enhancing zero-shot generalization performance on new tasks (Section 2.3). Furthermore, by simply fusing base-specific and task-shared knowledge in the two feature spaces at inference, we remarkably boost performance on the base task (Section 3.2).

Flexibility and Effectiveness. Our DePT framework is orthogonal to existing prompt tuning methods, so it can be flexibly used to overcome the BNT problem for them. We evaluate DePT on a broad spectrum of baseline methods, including the visual prompt tuning method VPT [6], textual prompt tuning methods CoOp [2], CoCoOp [3] and KgCoOp [4], and multi-model prompt tuning methods MaPLe [7], PromptSRC [8]. Experimental results on 11 diverse datasets show that DePT consistently improves the performance of these methods, regardless of whether there is a category shift, distribution shift or domain shift between base and new tasks, demonstrating its strong flexibility and effectiveness (Section 3.3). Notably, DePT enhances the six baselines without performance tradeoffs on base and new tasks – it achieves absolute gains of 1.31 % \thicksim 3.17 % (resp. 0.71 % \thicksim 2.23 %) on base (resp. new) tasks, averaged on the 11 datasets (Figure 1).

Contributions. Our main contributions are threefold. 1) We provide an analysis of the BNT problem in prompt tuning, revealing for the first time that the BNT stems from the channel bias issue. 2) We propose the DePT framework to tackle the BNT problem from a feature decoupling perspective; DePT is orthogonal to existing prompt tuning methods. 3) We perform experiments on 11 diverse datasets and show that DePT consistently enhances the performance of a broad spectrum of baseline methods.

References:
[1] Alec Radford, Jong Wook Kim, Chris Hallacy, Aditya Ramesh, Gabriel Goh, Sandhini Agarwal, Girish Sastry, Amanda Askell, Pamela Mishkin, Jack Clark, et al. Learning transferable visual models from natural language supervision. In ICML , pages 8748–8763, 2021.

[3] Kaiyang Zhou, Jingkang Yang, Chen Change Loy, and Ziwei Liu. Conditional prompt learning for vision-language models. In CVPR , pages 16816–16825, 2022b.
